title: The Piel and the Pual

objectives.can: Recognise and parse Piel and Pual forms.

explanation.summary: The Piel and the Pual are the two stems that double the middle root consonant. The Piel is active and very common; the Pual is its passive and rarer. What the Piel does to the sense of a verb differs from root to root, and for many of the commonest verbs of the Bible it is simply the stem in which the verb is used.

sections.heading: The shape of the Piel
body: The Piel doubles the middle root consonant in every form. The qatal has an i-vowel under the first root consonant and a second vowel after the doubled one: דִּבֶּר, שִׁלַּח. The yiqtol has a shewa under the person prefix: יְדַבֵּר, יְשַׁלַּח. The imperative and the infinitive construct have an a-vowel under the first root consonant and share a shape: דַּבֵּר, לְדַבֵּר. The participle has a prefixed mem with a shewa: מְדַבֵּר, מְשַׁלֵּחַ.

The vowel of the last syllable varies: it is often ṣere (as in דַּבֵּר, יְדַבֵּר) and patah in some forms, and it shortens before endings that begin with a consonant. Look first for the doubling and the vowel under the prefix or first consonant, not for the last vowel.

sections.heading: The Pual
body: The Pual is the same pattern with a u-vowel under the first root consonant and an a-vowel after the doubled consonant: שֻׁלַּח in the qatal, יְשֻׁלַּח in the yiqtol. The participle has the prefix mem with a shewa and a u-vowel: מְשֻׁלָּח. The Pual has no imperative and no infinitive construct in the analysed text, because commands are not passive; a single infinitive absolute occurs, in Genesis 40:15. In the analysed text the participles of the Pual are labelled 'passive participle', and they are often used as adjectives: מְבֹרָךְ.

The Pual is the passive of the Piel: Isaiah 50:1 puts the Piel שִׁלַּחְתִּיהָ ('I sent her away') beside the Pual שֻׁלְּחָה ('she was sent away'). For a few verbs the Pual is the passive of a verb whose active is in another stem, or of the Qal: יֻלַּד, 'was born'.

sections.heading: Roots that cannot double
body: Gutturals and resh do not take a doubling. When the middle root consonant is one of them, the vowel before it is lengthened instead, and the stem is recognised by the other marks. The Piel of the root with the sense 'bless' is the clearest example: בֵּרַךְ in the qatal and וַיְבָרֶךְ in the wayyiqtol have a long vowel where doubling would be expected. Genesis 2:3 puts it beside a normal Piel, וַיְקַדֵּשׁ, in the same verse.

sections.heading: What the Piel does to the sense
body: Grammarians describe several tendencies. With a root that means 'be' something, the Piel often means 'make something be so' (factitive): the Qal וַיִּגְדַּל means 'became great' in 1 Kings 10:23, and the Piel גִּדַּל means 'made great' in Esther 3:1. With some roots, the Piel means that the Qal's action is done to a large number, or repeatedly, or thoroughly. With some it comes from a noun: לְכַהֵן, 'to act as priest', is a Piel infinitive formed from the noun 'priest'. With some roots it reverses the Qal: the Qal 'learn' and the Piel 'teach' stand in Deuteronomy 4:10.

The old label 'intensive' fits only some verbs. For a large number of roots the Piel is simply the stem in which the verb occurs, with no contrast to draw: דִּבֶּר, 'speak', is a Piel (the Qal of its root is rare and found mainly in a few participles), and so are בִּקֵּשׁ, 'seek', and צִוָּה, 'command'. The Qal of the root of בֵּרַךְ occurs in the participle בָּרוּךְ, 'blessed', and almost nowhere else. For such verbs, learn the Piel as the verb. Do not look for an 'intensive' meaning in it.

sections.heading: Reading the Piel and the Pual
body: Spot the doubling, or the lengthened vowel where doubling is impossible. Then tell the Piel from the Pual by the vowels: i or a under the first consonant (or under the prefix, in the yiqtol, with a following a or e) points to the Piel; u points to the Pual. The Pual is rare, and a doubled form with a u-vowel under the first root consonant is almost always a Pual.

misunderstandings: The Piel does not mean 'intensive'. That fits some verbs; for others the Piel is factitive, denominative, or the ordinary form of the verb.
The doubled consonant is not always visible. A guttural or resh in the middle prevents it, and the vowel before it is lengthened.
The Piel and the Hiphil are not interchangeable, even where both can be translated with 'cause'. Each root has its own stems, and the lexicon records which.
The Pual is not a passive of every verb. It is the passive of the Piel, and rare; passives of the Qal are usually Niphals.

deeper.heading: Doubling and the Piel
body: The doubling is the mark of the stem. Hebrew grammars explain it differently: some see it as a lengthening of the action, which would explain the 'intensive' label, others as a pattern whose meaning has spread beyond that. The Hebrew of the Bible gives no direct evidence for choosing between them, and the practical rule is the one above: read the stem from its shape and its sense from the lexicon.

examples.analysis: Two Piel wayyiqtols. וַיְקַדֵּשׁ has the middle consonant doubled, with a shewa under the prefix after the wayyiqtol vav. וַיְבָרֶךְ has a long vowel where doubling would be expected, because the middle consonant is resh. Both are active, third masculine singular: God blessed the day and hallowed it.

examples.analysis: One root in two stems. יִלְמְדוּן is a Qal yiqtol, third masculine plural: 'they may learn'. יְלַמֵּדוּן is a Piel yiqtol, same person and number, with the middle consonant doubled: 'they may teach'.
